newsitem.title: USA: US jobless claims drop charged to seasonal factors.
newsitem.headline: US jobless claims drop charged to seasonal factors.

text.p: A sharp decline in U.S. jobless claims suggests U.S. labor markets are tight, but most of the falloff was attributed to distortions from seasonal factors in prior reports, analysts said.
On Thursday morning, the Labor Department said claims for state unemployment benefits in the week ended July 26 fell to 277,000, the lowest level since 269,000 the week concluding January 5, 1974.
U.S. economists in a Reuters poll had forecast 306,000 new claims would be filed.
Last week's reading on claims came in at 299,000, which was sharply below most economists' forecasts and hinted seasonal factors were at play amidst a tight labor market.
"It confirms that layoffs are not very big in the summer," said Astrid Adolfson, first vice president and an economist at MCM MoneyWatch.
"This is just confirmation of what we already know about the (labor market) tightness."
The department said 22 states and Puerto Rico reported decreases in claims exceeding 1,000 on an unadjusted basis in the week ended July 19.
Among the largest was Michigan, which reported 24,694 fewer initial claims for the week. Michigan attributed its decline to fewer layoffs in the automobile industry, the department said.
"The (drop) largely reflects the fact that the auto industry concentrated its model changeovers the first two weeks in July," said Michael Strauss, chief economist at Sanwa Securities (USA) Inc.
He said automobile manufacturers tend to concentrate their layoffs with model adjustments in the first two weeks of the month.
Nevertheless, Strauss said, "the dropoff in claims does suggest strength in the manufacturing sector, but not as great as the claims data imply."
The U.S. money market sold off slightly in the belly of the curve in the wake of the claims report. But after the data were digested, players bought on the dips.

Also, gross domestic product (GDP) data were released early in the morning. The Commerce Department said GDP rose 2.2 percent in the second quarter compared to a revised 4.9 percent in the first quarter.
At 0950 EDT/1350 GMT, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was up 15/32 at 104-13/32, to yield 6.29 percent.
